question.prompt: A 50 mm lens is focused at 3 m. A second row is 5 m away. Comparing depth of field at the same camera position and focus distance, which single change from f/4 increases depth of field?
question.expectedAnswer: Stop down the aperture to f/11
choices: Stop down the aperture to f/11
Switch to an 85mm lens at f/4
question.explanation: A smaller aperture increases depth of field, extending the zone of sharpness to cover both 3 m and 5 m. No other listed change affects depth of field.

choiceExplanations.Increase shutter speed to 1/1000s: Shutter speed does not affect depth of field; this only changes exposure.
choiceExplanations.Stop down the aperture to f/11: Correct: narrowing the aperture from f/4 to f/11 substantially increases depth of field.
choiceExplanations.Switch to an 85mm lens at f/4: A longer focal length at the same aperture and distance produces shallower depth of field, worsening the problem.
choiceExplanations.Raise ISO by 3 stops: ISO affects sensor sensitivity and noise, not depth of field.

sourceDocuments.name: Canon: depth of field (primary-source summary)
sourceDocuments.text: Depth of field depends on aperture, focal length, focus and shooting distance. With other conditions fixed, a smaller aperture increases depth of field; this qualitative change alone does not specify exact near and far sharpness limits.

sourceDocuments.name: Canon: exposure controls (primary-source summary)
sourceDocuments.text: Shutter duration affects both light exposure and motion rendering. ISO affects image brightness and noise; it does not directly change optical depth of field. Automatic modes may couple settings, so comparisons that change one optical variable should hold the others fixed.

bad_fields.quoted_text: No other listed change affects depth of field.
bad_fields.reason: The 85mm lens is another listed change affecting depth of field. It reduces rather than increases DoF under the controlled comparison; affecting is not the same as improving.

bad_fields.quoted_text: extending the zone of sharpness to cover both 3 m and 5 m
bad_fields.reason: The controlled task asks which change increases DoF. It does not supply enough optical/acceptable-blur information to guarantee that both specific distances become sharp.
Shutter duration also affects motion rendering, so this exclusive claim is false.

question.prompt: An alto saxophone is an E♭ transposing instrument: its written C sounds as concert E♭. A player reads a written G major triad (G, B, D). What triad is heard at concert pitch?
question.explanation: Alto sax written C = concert E♭, so each written note sounds a major sixth lower. Written G→B♭, B→D, D→F, yielding a concert B♭ major triad.

choiceExplanations.B♭ major: Correct: transposing each note of the written G major triad down a major sixth gives B♭, D, F.
choiceExplanations.E♭ major: Wrong: this would result from transposing only the root correctly and misapplying the interval to other notes.
choiceExplanations.F major: Wrong: no consistent transposition interval from G major produces F major.
choiceExplanations.C major: Wrong: this ignores the transposition entirely, as if concert pitch equaled written pitch.

sourceDocuments.name: Steps to Music Theory: transposing instruments (primary-source summary)
sourceDocuments.text: An E-flat alto saxophone sounds a major sixth below its written pitch. Transpose every chord note by the same interval. An interval can produce the same pitch class as another interval while differing by an octave.

sourceDocuments.name: Yamaha: saxophone transposition (primary-source summary)
sourceDocuments.text: Written C on an alto saxophone sounds as concert E-flat. On a B-flat tenor, written G major produces concert F major. Thus a G-major-to-F-major transposition is possible, although it is not the alto transposition in this task.

bad_fields.quoted_text: Wrong: this would result from transposing only the root correctly and misapplying the interval to other notes.

bad_fields.quoted_text: Wrong: this ignores the transposition entirely, as if concert pitch equaled written pitch.
bad_fields.reason: Ignoring transposition leaves G-B-D, hence G major, not C major.

question.explanation: A hash map lets you check in O(1) if (k - current) was already seen, achieving single-pass O(n) time with O(n) space for the map. Sorting takes O(n log n), nested loops are O(n²), and binary search per element is O(n log n).

question.prompt: For an arbitrary unsorted array of n integers, every matching index pair i < j must be explicitly listed. Can any method guarantee O(n) total time and O(n) auxiliary space for target k?
question.expectedAnswer: No: listing all matches alone can require quadratic time.
choices: No: listing all matches alone can require quadratic time.
Yes: a hash map guarantees O(n) time for listing every pair.
Yes: sorting and two pointers guarantee O(n) total time.
Yes: nested loops guarantee O(n) total time.
question.explanation: If all n values and k are zero, all n(n-1)/2 index pairs match. Writing that many outputs takes quadratic time, even with efficient lookup. O(n) auxiliary storage does not remove this output-time bound.

choiceExplanations.No: listing all matches alone can requir: With n zeroes and target zero, every pair of distinct indices matches. The quadratic number of required outputs rules out a linear total-time guarantee.
choiceExplanations.Yes: a hash map guarantees O(n) time for: Fast membership checks do not avoid emitting every match. One value can match many prior indices, so total time must include the output size.
choiceExplanations.Yes: sorting and two pointers guarantee: Comparison sorting is not generally linear; more importantly, explicitly listing all matches can still require quadratic time after sorting.
choiceExplanations.Yes: nested loops guarantee O(n) total t: Checking every unordered pair makes n(n-1)/2 checks. Nested loops therefore do not guarantee linear time.

choiceExplanations.F major: Wrong: no consistent transposition interval from G major produces F major.
choiceExplanations.C major: Wrong: this ignores the transposition entirely, as if concert pitch equaled written pitch.

question.prompt: You need to find all pairs in an unsorted array that sum to target k. Which approach gives O(n) time and O(n) space?
choices: Hash map storing complements seen so far
Binary search for each element's complement
question.expectedAnswer: Hash map storing complements seen so far
question.explanation: A hash map lets you check in O(1) if (k - current) was already seen, achieving single-pass O(n) time with O(n) space for the map. Sorting takes O(n log n), nested loops are O(n²), and binary search per element is O(n log n).

choiceExplanations.Hash map storing complements seen so far: Correct: constant-time complement lookup in a single pass finds all matching pairs in O(n) time using an O(n) map.
choiceExplanations.Sort then two-pointer scan: Comparison sorting generally costs O(n log n), so this method is slower than the stated linear-time hash-map solution.
choiceExplanations.Nested loop checking all pairs: Nested loops make quadratically many pair checks, so they do not match the linear-time hash-map solution.
choiceExplanations.Binary search for each element's complem: Sorting followed by a binary search for each complement generally requires O(n log n) time, rather than the linear-time hash-map solution.

question.prompt: For an arbitrary unsorted array of n integers, every matching index pair i < j must be explicitly listed. Can any method guarantee O(n) total time and O(n) auxiliary space for target k?
choices: No: listing all matches alone can require quadratic time.
Yes: a hash map guarantees O(n) time for listing every pair.
Yes: sorting and two pointers guarantee O(n) total time.
Yes: nested loops guarantee O(n) total time.
question.expectedAnswer: No: listing all matches alone can require quadratic time.
question.explanation: If all n values and k are zero, all n(n-1)/2 index pairs match. Writing that many outputs takes quadratic time, even with efficient lookup. O(n) auxiliary storage does not remove this output-time bound.

choiceExplanations.No: listing all matches alone can requir: With n zeroes and target zero, every pair of distinct indices matches. The quadratic number of required outputs rules out a linear total-time guarantee.
choiceExplanations.Yes: a hash map guarantees O(n) time for: Fast membership checks do not avoid emitting every match. One value can match many prior indices, so total time must include the output size.
choiceExplanations.Yes: sorting and two pointers guarantee: Comparison sorting is not generally linear; more importantly, explicitly listing all matches can still require quadratic time after sorting.
choiceExplanations.Yes: nested loops guarantee O(n) total t: Checking every unordered pair makes n(n-1)/2 checks. Nested loops therefore do not guarantee linear time.
